docs.title: Amelia (Moon)
docs.text: Not to be confused with Amelia the protagonist — the moon shares her name, and the coincidence has never been explained.

docs.title: Folk Tradition: The Daughter
docs.text:
In common folklore, Amelia is Maenar's daughter — the child who never leaves her father's side. She is smaller, softer, and eternally circling him. The folk rhyme says:

"Maenar walks the sky alone / Amelia follows, never gone. / One step behind, a hundred years / Her father's shadow dries her tears."

The pairing makes the twin moons a symbol of family, loyalty, and the bond between parent and child.

docs.title: The Green Mystery
docs.text:
Among rural folk, the green patches are called "Amelia's Veins" — believed to be the remnants of an ancient garden left by the gods. Some say that if you stare at Amelia long enough on a clear night, you can see the green move.

The Erisian church officially teaches that the green is a mineral phenomenon. Unofficially, they've never sent anyone to investigate.

docs.title: Erisian Church
docs.text: Amelia appears in Church iconography as the child-witness — present but silent, too young to speak of what she has seen. She represents innocence, potential, and the unknowable future. Her festivals are tied to spring and planting.

docs.title: 🕸️ Connections
docs.text: [ Amelia ] ├── Orbits: Maenar ├── Planet: Ge'or (via Maenar) ├── Rival Moon: Keg — the demon who wants to steal her ├── Folk Role: Daughter, the child, the green mystery ├── Surface: Faintly habitable — green patches, no seas ├── Religious Role: Innocence, spring, the future (Erisian church) └── Part Of: Ge'or — Moons

docs.title: 🔭 Modern Skepticism
docs.text:
Most educated Ge'orians dismiss Keg as folklore — a useful story to frighten children and explain the darkness of the sky. Astronomers point out that if Keg were truly moving closer, it would have been measured by now.

But the old elves still look over their shoulders on moonless nights.

And in the Ruins of Baoth, deep in the Archive of the Traveler, there is a star chart that maps Keg's orbit over the last fifteen thousand years.

It is closer than it was.

docs.title: 🕸️ Connections
docs.text: [ Keg ] ├── Orbits: Ge'or (distant) ├── Wants To Destroy: Maenar (jealousy) ├── Wants To Steal: Amelia ├── Folk Role: Demon moon, the jealous exile, the patient threat ├── Elven Tradition: Can only move during Maenar's dark phase ├── Dwarven Tradition: Tracked as a wandering blight ├── Church Stance: Pagan superstition (officially) └── Part Of: Ge'or — Moons

docs.title: Folk Tradition: The Father
docs.text:
In folklore across Erisdar, Maenar is the Father Moon — the steady, silent guardian who carries Amelia through the sky. He is old. He is tired. He has watched empires rise and fall. But he never stops walking the path, because if he stops, his daughter falls.

"Maenar does not rest. A father cannot." — Common saying in Central Erisdar

Together, Maenar and Amelia are called the Father and Daughter — a symbol of protection, duty, and the bond that outlasts all else.

docs.title: Elven Tradition
docs.text:
Maenar is the most sacred celestial body in elven culture. He is the Watcher of the Dead — believed to carry the souls of the departed across the sky until they can be reborn. Elven funerary rites are timed to Maenar's dark phase, when they say the veil between life and death is thinnest.

The dark surface patches — the Ancestors' Faces — are believed to be the shadows of great elven souls. Elders in the elvish states still recite the names of their lineage to Maenar on the night of a new moon.

docs.title: Erisian Church
docs.text: The Erisian church treats Maenar as a symbol of authority and protection — the father who shelters the innocent. But Church doctrine also keeps distance from the deeper elven traditions, which border on ancestor worship. In official iconography, Maenar is the shield; Amelia is the treasure held behind it.

docs.title: 🎭 Cultural Significance
docs.text:
• In Erisian church iconography, the ring is depicted as a divine halo around the world.
  • Elven traditions name it differently — calling it the "Veil of Lament" for the sister-moon that died to form it.
  • The folk pairing of Bride and Groom — beauty above, horror below — is one of the most enduring myths on Ge'or.
